cases.title: mqtt: drain queued output before advancing the state machine
cases.body:
A successful send can leave unsent bytes queued. Poll for writable events and drain those bytes before processing another packet. Wait for PUBLISH to drain before sending DISCONNECT, and for DISCONNECT to drain before completing the transfer.

Separate sending new packets from flushing queued bytes. Add unit coverage for partial, blocked and failed sends, plus MQTT/MQTTS integration tests. Update the test broker to handle fragmented reads.

Reported-by: OSS-Fuzz
Bug: https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/563679840, https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/559825608

cases.title: base64: avoid repeated input loads when encoding
cases.body:
This patch loads each three-byte input group into a `uint32_t` before writing the four encoded characters. Both standard and URL-safe base64 use this loop.

The ordering matters: it lets the compiler reuse the input in registers without proving that output stores cannot alias the input. The added comment documents that reason for the packed value.

## Assembly changes

The September 21 benchmark report includes before/after x86-64 disassembly from GCC 11.5.0 with `-O2 -DNDEBUG`. In that build, the original loop loads each input byte twice. These excerpts preserve instruction order but omit intervening instructions, as marked.

Before, input loads are interleaved with output stores:

```asm
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14]           ; input[0], first load
; ... advance pointers, calculate index 0, look up alphabet
mov   BYTE PTR [rdx-0x4],al        ; write output[0]
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14-0x3]       ; reload input[0]
movzx esi,BYTE PTR [r14-0x2]       ; input[1], first load
; ... calculate index 1, look up alphabet, write output[1]
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14-0x2]       ; reload input[1]
movzx esi,BYTE PTR [r14-0x1]       ; input[2], first load
; ... calculate index 2, look up alphabet, write output[2]
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14-0x1]       ; reload input[2]
```

After, each input byte is loaded once, before the first output store:

```asm
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14]           ; input[0], only load
; ... advance pointers and update remaining length
movzx edx,BYTE PTR [r14-0x2]       ; input[1], only load
shl   eax,0x10                    ; input[0] << 16
shl   edx,0x8                     ; input[1] << 8
or    eax,edx                     ; combine upper two bytes
movzx edx,BYTE PTR [r14-0x1]       ; input[2], only load
mov   edi,eax
shr   edi,0x12                    ; index 0
or    edx,eax                     ; complete 24-bit packed value
; ... calculate index 1 and look up alphabet[index 0]
mov   BYTE PTR [rsi-0x4],dil       ; first output store
```

The negative offsets refer to the current triplet because the loop advances the pointers early. The remaining indices come from register shifts and masks instead of further input loads. The first index does not need the third byte, so GCC calculates it before the final `or`. The old loop's two `cdqe` sign-extension instructions also disappear.

| Per complete input triplet | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Input-byte loads | 6 | 3 |
| Alphabet-table loads | 4 | 4 |
| Output-byte stores | 4 | 4 |
| Total load instructions | 10 | 7 |
| x86 instructions, including loop control | 34 | 28 |
| Loop machine-code size | 128 bytes | 101 bytes |

For the benchmark's 256-byte input, the loop processes 85 triplets; the unchanged tail handles the last byte. That removes 255 input-load instructions and 510 x86 instructions per call. These are instruction counts, not cycle counts or reductions in bytes fetched from RAM.

## Why the reloads?

The generated code is consistent with conservative alias analysis. Character-pointer accesses can alias, and allocation in the measured build goes through `Curl_cmalloc`, an indirect call that does not provide the compiler with the usual direct-`malloc` non-aliasing information.

Without proving that the output stores cannot affect the input, the compiler must preserve the original read-after-write behavior. Loading the triplet first makes reuse explicit in the C source. This explanation fits the disassembly; it was not verified with a compiler alias-analysis dump.

## Measured result

The report measured 153.359 ns before and 120.116 ns after: **21.68% less time**, with the after binary faster in all five paired rounds. Measurements used a static GCC build on an Intel Core Ultra 7 165H under WSL2, pinned to CPU 2, with compilation paused. Allocation and free remained part of the workload.

Those binaries included the report's other optimizations, so this is not an isolated measurement of this PR. Timings also shifted in unchanged routines. The disassembly demonstrates less work in this loop, but neither establishes a portable 22% gain nor attributes the timing improvement to individual instruction changes.

## Safety and tests

The implementation still performs three individual byte reads, avoiding alignment requirements, endian dependence, and reading beyond the triplet. Input bounds, allocation size, alphabets, padding, and one-/two-byte tail handling are unchanged. The loop remains scalar.

The added `unit1302` coverage checks binary prefixes of lengths 1–256, round-trip correctness, output lengths, and NUL termination. Existing vectors cover both alphabets and all remainder lengths. Local test 1302, source-style checks, and whitespace checks passed; the runner emitted missing-helper warnings for `curlinfo` and the server executable. The full suite and cross-platform checks were not run for this patch.

cases.title: mprintf: avoid scanning strings twice for unbounded %s
cases.body:
## Summary

Avoid scanning ordinary `%s` arguments twice in the shared formatter.

When precision is unspecified, `out_string()` already knows the exact string length, normally from `strlen()`. Previously, it passed that length to `stream_zrun()`, which scanned the same bytes again before forwarding them to `stream_run()`.

This patch sends known-length strings directly to `stream_run()`. Explicit precision still uses the existing bounded, NUL-aware scan. A flow comment explains why the two paths differ. This is one shared change benefiting `snprintf`, `maprintf`, and `simpleformat`, not three separate optimizations.

## Assembly justification

The September 21 benchmark report contains x86-64 disassembly from GCC 11.5.0 with `-O2 -DNDEBUG`. GCC inlined `out_string()` and `stream_zrun()` into `formatf()`. Both versions still call `strlen()` for nonempty strings with unspecified precision; the optimization removes the subsequent scan.

Before, the following consecutive instructions scan the string again. `r14` points to the string, `r10` holds its already-known length, and `r8` is the scan index:

```asm
40df8a: test  r10,r10                  ; zero length?
40df8d: je    40e302                   ; use an empty run
40df93: movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14]        ; reread first byte after strlen
40df97: xor   r8d,r8d                  ; scan index = 0
40df9a: jmp   40dfae
40df9c: nop   DWORD PTR [rax+0x0]       ; alignment
40dfa0: add   r8,0x1
40dfa4: cmp   r10,r8                   ; reached the already-known length?
40dfa7: jbe   40dfb2                   ; proceed to output
40dfa9: movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r14+r8*1]   ; reread next string byte
40dfae: test  al,al                    ; redundant NUL check
40dfb0: jne   40dfa0
```

After, a precision check bypasses that scan. In this version, `r11d` holds precision, `r13` holds length, and `r10` points to the string. The explicit-precision scan is omitted from this excerpt, as marked:

```asm
40df4c: cmp   r11d,0xffffffff          ; precision == -1?
40df50: je    40df73                   ; yes: skip the scan
; ... bounded, NUL-aware scan for explicit precision ...
40df73: mov   r8,r13                   ; pass the known length
40df76: mov   rcx,r10                  ; string
40df79: mov   rdx,r14                  ; block-output callback
40df7c: mov   rsi,rbx                  ; byte-output callback
40df7f: mov   rdi,r15                  ; sink state
40df82: mov   QWORD PTR [rsp+0x30],r9
40df87: call  40c970                   ; existing stream_run()
```

For each eligible string of length N, this removes N redundant byte reads, their NUL tests, and the associated scan-loop work, at the cost of a precision check. Width-only formats such as `%*s` also take this path: width does not impose a precision bound.

The initial length calculation and actual output copy remain. Fixed-buffer output still clamps writes to available space; allocating output retains its staging, size limits, and allocation handling. This does not introduce SIMD formatting or change the output callbacks.

## Recorded performance

The report measured five alternating before/after rounds pinned to CPU 2 on an Intel Core Ultra 7 165H under WSL2, with compilation paused. Both binaries used upstream revision `1ac826a1e064b94000820adc9ac187421ce4f0db` and a static GCC 11.5.0 `-O2 -DNDEBUG` build. Benchmark programs and inputs were unchanged.

| Benchmark | Before, ns/op | After, ns/op | Less time | Redundant byte reads removed/call |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `snprintf` | 327.640 | 306.017 | 6.60% | 23 |
| `maprintf` | 187.262 | 157.936 | 15.66% | 32 |
| `simpleformat` | 151.608 | 134.567 | 11.24% | 6 |

Each workload was faster in four of five paired rounds. The removed reads correspond to unspecified-precision string arguments only; they exclude `strlen()`, output copying, and literal-format handling. Allocation and free remain included in the allocating benchmark.

These are the report's measurements, not a new benchmark of this branch. The measured candidate also included base64 changes, and timings shifted in unchanged routines. The disassembly demonstrates elimination of the redundant scan, but the exact percentages are not isolated to this PR or guaranteed across compilers and platforms.

## Safety and validation

Explicit precision is a bound, not necessarily the string length. Its scan must stop at either NUL or the precision limit, preserving both short terminated strings and non-NUL-terminated `%.*s` buffers. Width, padding, truncation, NULL-string handling, positional arguments, and `%n` accounting remain unchanged.

The build and existing formatter tests **557 and 1398** passed. Their coverage includes precision limits, non-NUL-terminated input, padding, truncation, and the `va_list` variants, including allocating output. `checksrc` and `git diff --check` also passed. No additional tests were needed for these already-covered behaviors; the full suite, sanitizers, and cross-platform checks were not run for this patch.

cases.title: escape: use hex-pair lookup in curl_easy_escape
cases.body:
## Summary

Use a precomputed uppercase hex-pair table in `curl_easy_escape()`,
replacing two separate digit lookups with a two-byte `memcpy`.

Preserve literal-run batching, allocation bounds, character classification,
and NUL termination. The table adds 513 bytes before alignment. Using
`memcpy` avoids alignment, aliasing, and endianness assumptions.

Add regression coverage for all 256 byte values, checking exact encoded
output and decoded bytes, length, and termination.

## Performance

Saved measurements of this encoder change against baseline
`acec0de3921d2e5eb435410dbe4b2171b5097e9a`:

- GCC 11.5.0, `-O2 -DNDEBUG`, static libcurl, Intel Core Ultra 7 165H, WSL2.
- Five alternating baseline/candidate rounds, 3,000,000 calls each, pinned
  to CPU 2. Allocation and freeing remain inside the timed loop.
- Input contains all 256 byte values: 190 require escaping.
- Median `urlencode`: **248.942 → 186.344 ns/call**, **25.15% less time**.
  The candidate was faster in all five pairs.

These are earlier measurements, not a fresh benchmark of this branch.

**Caveat:** The unchanged `urldecode` benchmark was **8.69% slower**
(228.330 → 248.172 ns/call) in the same comparison. Code and table placement
changed, but the cause remains unproven. Further measurements on a native
host or with other compiler/link layouts are needed before claiming a net
performance improvement.

## Generated Assembly

GCC's x86-64 escaped-byte block, including loop-end control. Classification,
literal-run flushing, allocation, and termination are outside these excerpts.
At entry, `r12` holds the input byte and `rcx` points to its output slot.

### Before

```asm
mov   eax,r12d
and   r12d,0xf
mov   BYTE PTR [rcx],0x25
mov   rsi,rbx
shr   al,0x4
add   rcx,0x3
xor   r13d,r13d
and   eax,0xf
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [rax+0x4b5cc0]
mov   BYTE PTR [rcx-0x2],al
movzx eax,BYTE PTR [r12+0x4b5cc0]
mov   BYTE PTR [rcx-0x1],al
cmp   rbx,rbp
jne   40c389
```

### After

```asm
mov   BYTE PTR [rcx],0x25
mov   rsi,rbx
add   rcx,0x3
xor   r13d,r13d
movzx eax,WORD PTR [r12+r12*1+0x4b5640]
mov   WORD PTR [rcx-0x2],ax
cmp   rbx,rbp
jne   40c389
```

The block shrinks from **14 to 8 instructions**, with one table load instead
of two and two output stores instead of three. The two-byte `memcpy` is
inlined; output size is unchanged. These are instruction counts, not cycles.

## Validation

- Local Debug build and tests **543, 1396, 1560, and 1675** pass.
- Source-style and patch-whitespace checks pass.
- Full suite, fresh release benchmarks, and sanitizers were not run for this branch.

cases.title: X509 cert store cache never engages on builds with `CURL_CA_PATH` defined

label.rationale: Slop, hallucination, or vibe-coding language outside the project template.

cases.body:
### I did this

I have an app that uses the multi interface to send requests to 100–200 distinct hosts. For context, I was building curl myself with the BoringSSL backend and was using the multi interface with `CURLMOPT_MAXCONNECTS = 512`. Since I was just playing around at the time, I was using `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER = 0`.

I was seeing stable memory usage of 10–20 MB throughout the run. Then I set `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER = 1` back and added a CA using `CURLOPT_CAINFO`, and memory usage went up to ~200 MB with the same workflow as before. I then asked AI to debug it for me, and it found out that this happens because curl only caches the CA bundle when it comes from `CURL_CA_PATH` (which is picked up automatically when building curl) and never checks for cases like `CURLOPT_CAINFO`.

Below is the AI slop version of this bug report (there's a minimal reproducer there):

<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

## Summary

On builds where `CURL_CA_PATH` is defined (effectively every OpenSSL-based
Linux distro build), libcurl **re-parses the entire CA bundle into a private
`X509_STORE` on every new TLS connection**, because:

1. `vtls/vtls_config.c` (`Curl_ssl_filter_config_tmp_init()`) auto-fills the
   configure-time default `CURL_CA_PATH` into `ssl_filter_config.CApath`
   whenever the application has not called `CURLOPT_CAPATH` — *regardless of
   whether the application supplied its own CA via `CURLOPT_CAINFO` /
   `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` or relies on the build default CAfile*; and
2. `vtls/openssl.c` (`Curl_ssl_setup_x509_store()`) only caches the parsed
   `X509_STORE` in the multi handle if the config "comes exclusively from a
   CAfile", requiring `conn_config->CApath == NULL`.

Because the autofill makes `CApath` non-NULL for every connection, the cache
criteria can never be satisfied, and the X509 store cache — added specifically
to eliminate per-connection bundle parsing (commit `3c16697ebd`, "openssl:
reduce CA certificate bundle reparsing by caching", curl 7.86.0, closes #9620)
— is silently dead on default builds.

## Impact

- **Performance**: every connection re-reads and re-parses the full CA bundle
  (the Mozilla bundle is ~120–150 certificates). With connection pools
  holding hundreds of connections, this is the dominant setup cost.
- **Memory**: each idle connection retains its own parsed bundle
  (~500 KB/connection for a 189 KB PEM with 121 certs, measured with
  valgrind/massif). An application with 512 pooled connections to 512
  distinct hosts was measured at **562 MB RSS**; with the cache actually
  working, the same workload measured **52.6 MB RSS** (10.7x lower). The
  difference was almost entirely per-connection `X509`/`ASN1`/`RSA`
  allocations under `PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio`.
- **Not a security/correctness bug**: certificate verification always used a
  correct CA set; only redundancy is wasted.

## Reproduce

The store is cached in the **multi handle**, so the repro must use a single
multi with multiple concurrent connections:

```c
/* repro.c — two transfers, one multi handle */
#include <string.h>
#include <curl/curl.h>

static size_t write_cb(void *p, size_t s, size_t n, void *u) {
    (void)p; (void)u; return s * n;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *urls[2] = {"https://example.com/", "https://httpbin.org/get"};
    CURL *e[2];
    CURLM *m = curl_multi_init();
    int still = 0, i;

    for(i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        e[i] = curl_easy_init();
        curl_easy_setopt(e[i], CURLOPT_URL, urls[i]);
        curl_easy_setopt(e[i], CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION, write_cb);
        curl_easy_setopt(e[i], CURLOPT_CAINFO,
                         "/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt");
        curl_multi_add_handle(m, e[i]);
    }

    do {
        curl_multi_perform(m, &still);
        if(still)
            curl_multi_poll(m, NULL, 0, 1000, NULL);
        do {
            int left;
            CURLMsg *msg = curl_multi_info_read(m, &left);
            if(!msg) break;
            if(msg->msg == CURLMSG_DONE)
                curl_multi_remove_handle(m, msg->easy_handle);
        } while(1);
    } while(still);

    for(i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        curl_easy_cleanup(e[i]);
    curl_multi_cleanup(m);
    return 0;
}
```

Count how often the CA bundle file is opened:

```
$ gcc repro.c -lcurl -o repro
$ strace -f -e trace=openat -o trace.log ./repro
$ grep -c "openat.*ca-certificates.crt" trace.log
2                       # actual: parsed once per connection
```

Expected: **1** — the second connection should reuse the cached store from
the shared multi handle.

## Verified on

| Build | CA set by app | Bundle parses (2 conns, 1 multi) |
|---|---|---|
| curl master 8.23.0-DEV (2026-10-11, CMake defaults: `CURL_CA_PATH="/etc/ssl/certs"`) | `CURLOPT_CAINFO` | **2** |
| curl master 8.23.0-DEV, + fix option 2 below | `CURLOPT_CAINFO` | **1** |
| curl master 8.23.0-DEV, + fix option 2 below | default (autofilled CAfile) | **2** (option 2 does not cover this case) |
| Ubuntu curl 8.18.0 (OpenSSL/3.5.5, stock distro build) | `CURLOPT_CAINFO` | **2** |
| Ubuntu curl 8.18.0 (stock distro build) | default | **2** |

## Root cause

`lib/vtls/vtls_config.c`, `Curl_ssl_filter_config_tmp_init()` — autofill only
checks whether *this particular option* was customized by the app:

```c
#ifdef CURL_CA_PATH
    if(!sslc->custom_capath && !CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SSL_CAPATH)) {
      result = Curl_setstropt(data, STRING_SSL_CAPATH, CURL_CA_PATH);
```

`lib/vtls/openssl.c`, `Curl_ssl_setup_x509_store()` — cache requires the
config to come exclusively from a CAfile:

```c
  cache_criteria_met = (data->set.ssl_ca_cache_timeout != 0) &&
    conn_config->verifypeer &&
    !conn_config->CApath &&          /* <-- always false after autofill */
    !conn_config->ca_info_blob &&
    !conn_config->CRLfile &&
    !conn_config->native_ca_store;
```

Runtime confirmation on master (temporary `infof` added to the criteria
evaluation, two transfers on one multi):

```
* x509cache: met=0 timeout=86400 verifypeer=1 CApath=0x5dfc61940510 blob=(nil) ...
* x509cache: met=0 timeout=86400 verifypeer=1 CApath=0x5dfc619411e0 blob=(nil) ...
```

(the same `CURLOPT_CAINFO` on every handle; `CApath` autofilled per
connection, criteria never met). With the autofill suppressed, the same
run shows `met=1`, the second connection picks up the cached store, and the
bundle is read once.

Note `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` is excluded from caching for a separate, sensible
reason (blobs have no comparable identity for the cache key, and a
`NULL == NULL` CAfile match would falsely equate *different* blobs). This
report is about the `CApath` autofill defeating the cache — including the
default-config case where the app relies on the build default CAfile, which
is the common case.

## Suggested fixes

Two possible directions:

1. **Include `CApath` in the cache identity** (recommended — no behavior
   change, covers all cases): store `CApath` alongside `CAfile` in
   `ossl_x509_share`, compare both in `ossl_cached_x509_store_different()`,
   and drop the `!conn_config->CApath` term from the criteria. The store
   remains shared for connections whose `(CAfile, CApath)` pair matches —
   which is the normal case, since both come from the same configure-time
   defaults. The reason for the strict exclusivity (CA directory contents can
   change without the path string changing) can be handled by the existing
   `CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT` expiry, same as it already handles a CAfile
   whose contents change on disk.
2. **Skip the `CURL_CA_PATH` autofill when the app supplied any custom CA**
   (small behavior change): mirror the existing
   `USE_APPLE_SECTRUST`/`CURL_CA_NATIVE` guard:

   ```c
   if(!sslc->custom_capath && !sslc->custom_cafile && !sslc->custom_cablob &&
      !CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SSL_CAPATH)) {
   ```

   Applications that set `CURLOPT_CAINFO` then verify exclusively against
   the CA they specified (arguably matching intent), and the cache engages.
   Verified working on master for the app-supplied-CAINFO case (table above),
   but it does not help the default-CA configuration, which is why option 1
   is preferred.

## Environment

- curl master 8.23.0-DEV (2026-10-11), CMake default build, OpenSSL/3.5.5,
  `CURL_CA_PATH="/etc/ssl/certs"` — reproduced and root-caused with runtime
  instrumentation
- Ubuntu stock curl 8.18.0 (libcurl/8.18.0 OpenSSL/3.5.5) — reproduced

</details>


### I expected the following

Proper CA bundle reuse.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.23.0-DEV (b8f71d6e1199701352c498467c17847237d1c43e)

### operating system

Linux localhost 7.0.0-1012 #12-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT Thu Aug  6 19:23:26 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux

Updates `filelock` from 3.32.7 to 4.0.12
Release notes

Sourced from filelock's releases.

4.0.12

  • Fix read-lock acquisition on SQLite versions older than 3.33.0 by using sqlite_master for the schema probe. #769

PyPI release

Full Changelog: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/compare/4.0.11...4.0.12

4.0.11

  • ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock use a validated private hard link when /dev/fd has no entry for the database descriptor, supporting NetBSD's static descriptor directory beyond descriptor 63. The temporary location must share a filesystem with the database. The symlink refusal test accepts NetBSD's error wording.

PyPI release

Full Changelog: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/compare/4.0.10...4.0.11

4.0.10

  • Reusing a singleton AsyncFileLock with another loop, executor or run_in_executor, or a singleton SoftFileLease with another lease_duration, heartbeat_interval or on_compromise, now raises ValueError instead of returning the lock with its original options. #765

PyPI release

Full Changelog: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/compare/4.0.9...4.0.10

4.0.9

  • ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock close the descriptor that checks the database path once SQLite has connected, so on PyPy a dropped lock leaves no descriptor open until garbage collection runs. #763
  • ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock refuse a symlink at the database path instead of following it, so a user who can create names in a shared lock directory cannot point the lock at another file (GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56).

PyPI release

Full Changelog: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/compare/4.0.8...4.0.9

4.0.8

  • ReadWriteLock.release() and SoftReadWriteLock.release() from a thread that does not hold the write lock now raise RuntimeError instead of dropping the holder's lock and letting a second writer in. #761

PyPI release

Full Changelog: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/compare/4.0.7...4.0.8

4.0.7

  • File locks now raise ValueError at construction when mode denies the owner read or write, such as mode=0o444, instead of failing on a later acquire and staying broken until someone deletes the lock file. #760

  • Creating a lock on a Python 3.15 interpreter without types.LazyImportType no longer triggers AttributeError at exit. :pr:860
  • Handle EFTYPE when a no-follow open refuses a symlink in a soft reader/writer lock's protocol tree, so heartbeat reports lost ownership rather than a transient refresh error.

4.2.2 (2026-10-18)

  • Fix a lock on a relative path that stayed held after a later with lock: ended, when an earlier acquire() had failed because the working directory no longer exists. That call still raises :class:FileNotFoundError, and it now leaves the lock's hold count unchanged. :pr:856

4.2.1 (2026-10-17)

  • On a singleton wrapper, :meth:AsyncReadWriteLock.close() <filelock.AsyncReadWriteLock.close> and :meth:AsyncSoftReadWriteLock.close() <filelock.AsyncSoftReadWriteLock.close> end only the holds that tasks acquired through that wrapper. A reader that arrives during close() gets the closed error instead of joining the ending hold. After synchronous code closes or force-releases the shared lock, the wrappers refuse to admit readers into the ended hold, and close() on such a wrapper returns. Closing one wrapper no longer ends a task's nested hold taken through another wrapper on the same path. :pr:832
  • :class:~filelock.ReadWriteLock locks again after a release() that an exception from a signal handler interrupted. The async read-write wrappers stop admitting readers into such a level. The async read-write locks forget a hold whose backend release failed after the backend let go, and they free the memory of each acquire that times out or is canceled. :class:~filelock.AsyncFileLock returns from release() after a few hundred acquires gave up behind a waiting one. An exception from a signal handler delivered while an :class:~filelock.AsyncFileLock call joins its queue no longer blocks every later call on that lock. :pr:833
  • Fix :class:~filelock.ReadWriteLock acting on -journal, -wal or -shm files another process puts beside its database: a write could land in another file, a reader could get in beside a writer, and an acquire could fail. SQLite now opens the database by name only in a directory no other account can write, and through a private hard link elsewhere. On Windows the directory's access control list decides.
